about: The Epistle of the Sixth Sunday after Epiphany in the 1962 Roman Missal, also used when this formulary is resumed after Pentecost. Paul gives thanks for the Thessalonians’ faith and describes how they turned from idols to the living God and await His Son. Their reception of the Gospel becomes an example for believers elsewhere.

seg.tr: Brethren: We thank God at all times for every one of you, calling you to mind in our prayers without ceasing, mindful of the work of your faith, and of labor, and of love, and of the endurance of the hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, before God and our Father. And we know, brethren beloved of God, that you have been chosen, because our Gospel did not reach you in speech alone, but in power as well, and in the Holy Spirit, and in much fullness, as you know what we were like among you for your sake. And you have become our imitators, and the Lord’s, welcoming the word in much distress, with joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you have been made an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia. For it is from you that the word of the Lord has spread abroad, not only in Macedonia and in Achaia, but your faith toward God has also gone out into every place, so that there is no need for us to say anything. For they themselves tell about us the manner of our coming to you, and how you turned from idols to God, to be servants of the living and true God, and to be waiting for His Son from the heavens (whom He raised from among the dead), Jesus, who has rescued us from the wrath that is to come.

a.g: the word of the Lord has been spread abroad
your faith, which is directed toward God, has spread everywhere
what our coming to you was like

ex.w022: Labor and love are separately joined by et in this Latin wording. Both belong to the things Paul remembers in prayer.
ex.w037: The speakers who give thanks also know the recipients’ being chosen. The intervening address, brethren beloved by God, names the recipients and God as the one who loves them, not as an agent of knowing.
ex.w064: Plenitúdo means fullness. The corresponding Greek word in this passage means full assurance or conviction, which suggests that the fullness here is the full conviction with which the Gospel came.
ex.w106: Here diffamátus est means that the Lord’s word has spread and become widely known. It carries no suggestion of slander.
ex.w167: The parenthetical clause refers to the Son: God raised Him from the dead. Jesus is then named as the one who rescued us, while the wrath is still described as coming.
